# Books and bookshelves

These are fictional records supplied for this exercise. A database persists
stored rows; rendering those rows into the page only changes a view.

bookshelves

| id | label |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Fiction |
| 2 | Science |

books

| id | title | shelf_id |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | Moon Map | 1 |
| 11 | River Robots | 1 |
| 12 | Seed Lab | 2 |

Draw two boxes for these tables. Each id is a primary key, unique within
its table. Each books.shelf_id is a foreign key referring to bookshelves.id.
One shelf has many books; every book here belongs to one existing shelf.
library.sql supplies the schema, constraints, rows and two read queries.
You can predict their results without installing a database.

SELECT chooses output columns; FROM chooses source rows; WHERE filters
rows. Query A selects title from books with shelf_id=1, ordered by id:
Moon Map
River Robots

JOIN combines rows whose shelf IDs match. Query B returns:
Moon Map | Fiction
River Robots | Fiction
Seed Lab | Science

Write each predicted result before comparing it with these worked results.
Then explain the same join as a JavaScript lookup by shelf_id.

CRUD describes create, read, update and delete:
CREATE: INSERT INTO books VALUES (13,'Star Garden',2);
READ: SELECT title FROM books WHERE id=13; gives Star Garden.
UPDATE: UPDATE books SET shelf_id=1 WHERE id=13;
READ the join again: Star Garden now pairs with Fiction.
DELETE: DELETE FROM books WHERE id=13;
READ again: the three original books remain.

Run this sequence beginning from library.sql. Changing only a
displayed title leaves a stored row unchanged. Changing an in-memory
JavaScript array lasts only in that program until deliberately saved;
a SQL UPDATE changes stored data. Explain which action each example performs.
An insert using shelf_id=99 fails the foreign-key constraint. A repeated
primary-key id fails its uniqueness constraint. Record both predictions.

If SQLite is available, run library.sql in a temporary database, then the
CRUD sequence above. Otherwise retain the diagram, query predictions and
worked comparisons as the complete local artifact. An optional online
schema diagram can reproduce these fictional tables after this work.

# Check-In 2: Helpers, Events, APIs and Data

Continue the same Core project across Helpers, APIs and Databases. Open
index.html directly. The interface, request helper and fixtures are supplied;
complete the three functions in helpers.js before comparing the reference.

## Helpers and event coordinates

Implement sumEvens(values) with a named helper and a reduce total starting
at 0. Preserve the input array. The original arrays [2,1,6,91,-1] and
[0,3,2,91,-1] give 8 and 2. Also check [] gives 0, [1,2] gives 2,
[-3,2] gives 2, and [-4,2] gives -2. Starting reduce without 0 would
fail for [] and incorrectly include an odd first element.

Implement canvasPoint(event,canvas). Read canvas.getBoundingClientRect(),
subtract rect.left and rect.top from clientX and clientY, then multiply
each coordinate by its buffer-size/display-size ratio:
x = (clientX - left) * canvas.width / rect.width
y = (clientY - top) * canvas.height / rect.height
A 500 by 500 buffer displayed at 250 by 250, with left=40 and top=60,
maps click (165,185) to (250,250). The top-left maps to (0,0).
The page deliberately scales the canvas. Click near the center and an edge,
then compare the visible position with the reported buffer coordinates.

## API data

fixture.js is a small authored practice object shaped like a move-list
response. It is supplied with this project, rather than fetched on opening.
Implement firstMove(data): call checkpointRemote.validateList(data) and
return data.results[0].name. The fixture's first name is pound. Invalid,
missing or empty results must produce a useful error instead of a crash.

Use practice fixture to display that result. Request 20 move names is
optional and performs one public GET to the documented move-list endpoint.
The supplied remote.js checks response.ok, parses JSON, validates before
caching, and uses AbortController to abort after five seconds. Inspect how
loading, request, validation, state and display have separate responsibilities.
Repeated successful reads use the page's memory cache. Reload clears it.
An offline, non-OK, malformed or timeout response must retain the last valid
name and source label while displaying an error. Avoid private records.

## Database worksheet

Read DATABASE.md and library.sql. Both complete tables, keys, queries and
worked results are provided locally. Predict SELECT/WHERE and JOIN outputs,
draw their relationship, and walk through the supplied CRUD sequence.
Distinguish changing a view, an in-memory array and stored database rows.
SQLite execution and a hosted diagram are optional.

## Completion

Retain expected and observed fixed sums, original-array preservation, two
canvas clicks with coordinate predictions, fixture output, and a database
diagram with query/CRUD predictions. If trying live requests, record the
visible source and recovery result. Change one input, predict its output,
then keep the observed result. Continue across tasks with these saved files.

# Move Analyzer

Build a page that groups move objects by their nested type.name and counts
the form-selected type. The complete local fixture and page controls are
supplied. Open index.html directly and complete moves.js.

fixture.js contains six authored practice records with fictional move names
and the same nested name/type.name structure used by PokéAPI move objects.
The expected counts are fire=2, water=2, normal=1 and electric=1. This is a
six-record sample; its counts do not describe the complete API collection.

Implement countTypes(moves): call moveData.validateMoves, loop over moves,
read each move.type.name, and increment the matching counter. Return the
counts without changing the supplied array. Object.create(null) gives a
dictionary without inherited property names. The four counts sum to six.

Implement countForType(counts,input): convert input to a string, trim spaces
and lowercase it. Empty input produces Enter a move type; an unrecognized
type produces an Unknown move type message. moveData.types supplies the
recognized types. A valid type absent from the sample has count0.
Return {type:key,count:number} and let the supplied interface render it with
textContent. Avoid a prompt loop or HTML interpolation.

Use six-move practice fixture, then submit Fire, water, " WATER ", grass,
an empty input and an unknown type. Expected: 2,2,2,0,empty-input message,
unknown-type message. Compare the visible counts with the same six records
and check that their names and nested types remain unchanged.

## Optional live data

Request moves 1 through 6 is an explicit optional action. The supplied
data.js reads these six fixed IDs sequentially, one GET at a time. Every
response must have a move name and a recognized type.name. remote.js
checks HTTP status, parses JSON, validates before caching and aborts each
request after five seconds. Six requests are the fixed maximum for a new
complete sample. A second successful read reuses those cached responses
until reload. No requests run just by opening or typing into the page.

Counts become current only after all six records succeed. If any request
fails, the last valid sample, counts and source label remain visible with
an error. A failed response is not cached. Describe what happens for offline,
timeout, non-OK and malformed responses; use the local fixture whenever a
live request is unavailable. Compare types within the actual returned sample,
rather than assuming it matches the practice fixture or all available moves.

## Completion

Keep the six practice inputs and results, original data, counts summing to
six, source label and a changed fixture with its predicted counts. If using
live data, retain its visible source and a failed-refresh recovery result.
Explain why ready must wait for every selected request, why one last-numbered
request finishing does not establish that others finished, and how caching
and the fixed request bound keep this project responsive.
